title: How to Verify an FBR Invoice in Pakistan
metaDescription: How to verify an FBR invoice in Pakistan — scan the QR code or enter the invoice number on the FBR portal to confirm a sale was reported, and what to do if it fails.
content:
Verifying an FBR invoice, defined

Verifying an FBR invoice means confirming, on the FBR portal, that the sale behind the receipt was genuinely reported to the FBR IRIS system. In practice you scan the QR code on the invoice, or enter its number on the FBR verification page, and check that it resolves to a real record. This matters more than most people realise: a receipt can print perfectly at the counter while the sale never reached FBR at all. Verification is the only way to tell a genuinely compliant invoice from one that just looks the part.

For customers it is proof they received a valid tax invoice. For businesses it is the fastest way to catch silent reporting failures before they turn into penalties. This guide covers both — how to verify, what the results mean, and what to do when an invoice does not check out.

Why verification matters

The whole point of Pakistan's QR-invoicing requirement is verifiability. When a sale is reported to IRIS in real time, FBR returns a reference that the point of sale encodes into the QR code. Anyone can then confirm the sale exists in FBR's records. If the QR does not verify, the sale is effectively invisible to FBR — and for a registered business, invisible sales are unreported sales, with penalties that start around PKR 10,000 and climb for repeat offences.

How to verify an FBR invoice

There are two simple methods, and either works:

  1. Scan the QR code on the receipt with your phone camera — it opens the FBR verification result directly.
  2. Or open the FBR verification page on the FBR website if you prefer entering details manually.
  3. Enter the invoice number printed on the receipt if prompted.
  4. Review the result — a valid invoice shows the seller and sale details recorded in IRIS.
  5. Note a "not found" result — this means the invoice is not in FBR's records and was not properly reported.

Verification takes seconds and needs no login for a basic check. Businesses should make a habit of scanning a few of their own receipts regularly to confirm the integration is genuinely working.

What the result tells you

ResultWhat it meansAction
Invoice found, details matchSale was reported to FBRNone — it is valid
Invoice not foundSale not reported to IRISBusiness must investigate
Details do not matchWrong data reportedCheck tax mapping / POS

Why an invoice fails verification

When a valid-looking receipt will not verify, the cause is almost always a failed submission that printed anyway. The most common reasons are an expired FBR IRIS authentication token — these expire roughly every 60 minutes, so a POS that does not refresh them stops reporting after the first hour — or a dropped connection whose invoices never synced. In both cases the QR encodes a reference that simply does not exist in IRIS. Understanding this is what turns a mysterious "not found" into a fixable problem; our guide to common FBR POS issues covers each cause and its fix.

What businesses should do about failed verifications

For a business, an invoice that fails verification is not a curiosity — it is a warning that sales are going unreported. Treat it as urgent:

  • Check the IRIS dashboard to see how many recent invoices are actually recorded.
  • Identify the cause — usually token refresh or offline sync — and fix it.
  • Re-submit the affected invoices so the sales are reported.
  • Reconcile monthly going forward so a gap can never build up unnoticed.

A real example

A customer at an electronics shop in Rawalpindi scanned their receipt out of curiosity and got "invoice not found." When they mentioned it, the owner discovered the POS token had expired mid-morning, and every afternoon sale that day had failed to report — a silent gap that, at that volume, risked a penalty running past PKR 100,000. Because a single scan surfaced it, the shop fixed the token setting and re-submitted the day's invoices before it became an enforcement matter.

The habit worth building

Verification is the cheapest compliance check there is. Customers can confirm they got a real invoice, and businesses can catch silent failures in seconds rather than discovering them in an audit. To understand how the QR gets created in the first place, see how to generate FBR QR invoices, and for the mechanics behind reporting, how the FBR POS invoicing system works. Treat the IRIS record — not the printed receipt — as the truth, and verification becomes a quick, powerful safeguard.

faqs.question: What does verifying an FBR invoice mean?
faqs.answer: Verifying an FBR invoice means confirming, on the FBR portal, that the sale was genuinely reported to the IRIS system. A verified invoice resolves to a real IRIS record; an unverifiable one means the sale may never have reached FBR, regardless of what the printed receipt shows.

faqs.question: How do I verify an FBR invoice as a customer?
faqs.answer: Scan the QR code on the receipt with your phone, or visit the FBR verification page and enter the invoice number. A valid result shows the recorded sale details; 'not found' means the invoice was not properly reported to FBR.

faqs.question: Why would a valid-looking invoice fail verification?
faqs.answer: Usually because the submission to FBR IRIS failed but the receipt still printed — often due to an expired authentication token or a dropped connection. The QR then encodes a reference that does not exist in IRIS, so it cannot be verified.

faqs.question: What should a business do if its invoices fail verification?
faqs.answer: Treat it as a compliance emergency: the sales were likely not reported. Check your IRIS dashboard, fix the cause (commonly token refresh or offline sync), re-submit affected invoices, and add a monthly reconciliation so it does not recur.

faqs.question: Does a printed receipt prove FBR compliance?
faqs.answer: No. A receipt can print even when the submission to IRIS failed. Only a QR that verifies against a real IRIS record proves the sale was reported — which is exactly why verification matters.
